The software is intended to act as a single layer for managing AI activity, costs, identity and oversight across different models, tools and teams. It forms part of Globant's broader AI services approach, which combines software with human-supervised delivery teams known as AI Pods. Glob.AI OS connects to more than 320 open and closed AI models from more than 25 providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The system can direct tasks to different models while giving companies visibility into spending, usage and policy controls. The product is built around four parts: an Intelligence Hub for model access and routing, a Corporate Hub for linking company data and systems, an Agentic Hub for testing and running AI agents, and a Token Vault for budgets, permissions and audit records. It can be deployed as software as a service or within a client's own cloud environment. Access is available through chat, web, desktop and command-line interfaces, as well as through headless deployment using MCP. Glob.AI OS is intended to bring governed AI into day-to-day work rather than limit it to specialist teams. Through what Globant calls Glob.AI Apps, employees can use AI tools in existing workflows, ask questions, delegate tasks, work with coding agents and use prebuilt agentic systems from Globant and partners. **Services model** The launch also highlights a shift in how Globant wants to sell AI-related work to large clients. Rather than charging by hours worked or software seats, customers can pay for outcomes or consumption through its AI-Native Services model. That model combines AI Pods, which Globant describes as human-supervised delivery units, with the new operating layer. The pods bring together documented workflows, AI agents and oversight from specialists, including Forward Deployed Engineers, while the operating system provides governance and shared access to data, controls and institutional knowledge. Globant argues that many companies have already adopted AI tools in fragmented ways, with multiple teams using different models and systems tied to sensitive data. In that environment, the challenge is less about gaining access to AI and more about controlling its use at scale and tying it to production work. "We are making it seamless for global leaders to take the best out of AI leveraging Globant's 23+ years of experience working with top companies in almost every industry in a completely reshuffled engagement model where they only pay for outcomes," said Sarab Narang, Chief Executive Officer of Glob.AI. The reported gains depend on internal evaluations and hardware-specific measurements that outside testers still need to reproduce. Edge0 released [Edge0-145B](https://edge0.ai/blog/introducing-edge0-145b-frontier-ai-capabilities-on-your-own-computer), a 145-billion-parameter language model the company says runs on a personal computer. The release includes Edge0-120B, an inference framework, deployment tools, and model weights on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co), with code and guides on [GitHub](https://github.com). Edge0 positions the models for coding, reasoning, and agent workflows without sending prompts to a cloud model. ## What's claimed Edge0 describes Edge0-145B as an open-source on-device model with 145 billion parameters and performance near specific frontier cloud models. In the company's laptop tests, the model reached peak memory of 29 gigabytes, prompt processing above 1,100 tokens per second, generation above 80 tokens per second, and power draw near 120 watts. Edge0 reports support for 128,000 to 256,000 tokens of context on long inputs. Edge0 also claims the model can complete multi-step work on a local machine. The company points to demonstrations in which Edge0-145B planned tasks, wrote and ran code, debugged failures, and inspected results. Examples include 3D scenes in Blender, game assets, drone control code, and a printed circuit board workflow in KiCad and Unreal Engine 5. ## What's new The release combines model architecture and inference engineering aimed at the limits of laptop memory and bandwidth. Edge0 says it shares large matrices across groups of sparse experts, trains the model in its on-device form from the start, pipelines data across GPU memory, system memory, and SSD storage, and splits work between the CPU and GPU with speculative decoding. Of the 145 billion parameters, Edge0 reports that about 10 billion participate in each inference step. Edge0 presents benchmark results from its internal evaluations. In the company's table, Edge0-145B scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1, 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 35.4 on HLE, 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond, 80.6 on IFBench, and 79.3 on AA-LCR. Edge0 compares those scores with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, and Claude-Opus-4.6 (Max), with gaps in published results marked by dashes. The memory comparison stands out. Edge0 reports 29 gigabytes of measured peak memory for Edge0-145B on a laptop, against estimated 70-gigabyte and 87-gigabyte footprints for standard 4-bit deployments of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. Edge0 says this makes the model usable on a 48-gigabyte laptop. The company states that it will release the evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions with a technical report. Edge0 frames local inference as a way to avoid cloud-model token or API fees, keep code and documents on the user's hardware, and continue core tasks offline. The company also describes a broader portfolio of 200 models across four families, with day-one Edge0-145B support on macOS, Windows, and Linux, including Apple M-series chips and NVIDIA hardware such as RTX Spark, RTX 4090, and RTX 5090. ## Limitations The results in Edge0...

AI Basics and How-To Guides # GLM vs Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok and DeepSeek: How Zhipu’s Open Model Compares By [Lenka Vojtechova](/author/lenka-vojtechova/)  ·  Updated November 11, 2026  ·  13 min read [AI Coding](/tag/ai-coding/)[Claude](/tag/claude/)[DeepSeek](/tag/deepseek/)[Fello AI](/tag/fello-ai/)[GLM](/tag/glm/)[LLM](/tag/llm/)[Gemini](/tag/gemini/)[Grok](/tag/grok/) ![GLM vs Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and DeepSeek thumbnail showing a glowing GLM-5.2 logo facing a grid of rival AI model icons in a dark cinematic neon background.](/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GLM-vs-other-ai-1536x864-hero.webp) **GLM vs Claude** is the question people search, and the 2026 answer starts with a correction: the GLM worth comparing is no longer GLM-5.2. Z.ai now sells three of them, and on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index **v5.0.1**, read on November 11, 2026, the flagship **[GLM-5.3](/glm-5-3/)** scores **31.7** and **[GLM-5.3 Flash](/glm-5-3-flash/)** scores **27.8**, while the older **[GLM-5.2](/glm-5-2/)** has **no v5 score at all** on an identical **$1.40 / $4.40** rate card. Against **[Claude Opus 5.5](/claude-opus-5-5/)** at **$4 / $20**, GLM-5.3 is 2.9x cheaper on input and 4.5x on output, and that gap is what this whole comparison turns on. So the real question is not just GLM vs Claude. It is whether an open-weight model at a fraction of the cost can stand in for any of the big paid flagships. This guide compares **GLM-5.3** and the far cheaper **GLM-5.3 Flash** head-to-head with **Claude, GPT-6, Gemini, Grok and DeepSeek** on price, benchmarks, context and coding, then tells you which model to pick for which job. Every score below was re-read from the Artificial Analysis model pages on **November 11, 2026**, and every price comes from the vendors’ own pricing pages. One thing to settle first, because the licences differ inside the family: GLM-5.2 and GLM-5.3 Flash ship under **MIT**, while GLM-5.3’s weights are public under **Z.ai’s own GLM-5.3 License**, permissive except for cloud operators above $10 billion in revenue. ## The Key Takeaways > * **GLM-5.3 Flash is the cheapest GLM to run, but no longer the value pick.** At $0.15 / $0.50 per million tokens it costs $0.58 per Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index task and scores 27.8, while Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro scores 29.9 for $0.26 a task and GPT-6 Luna matches Flash’s score for $0.15. What Flash keeps is a flat rate and an MIT licence. > * **Claude still wins the hardest agentic work, by a wider margin than before.** Claude Opus 5.5 scores 59.1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1 and Claude Fable 5.2 leads the whole board at 64.6, against GLM-5.3’s 31.7. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Best Local LLM for Coding: $0 Weights vs $2 API [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Nov 12, 2026 · 26 min read The best local LLM for coding in mid-November 2026 depends less on a leaderboard score than on three constraints: how much memory your machine has, what license the weights carry, and whether you can verify the files you download. Google’s [Gemma 4 family, released under Apache 2.0 with commercial use allowed](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemma-4/), OpenAI’s gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b, and Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro all compete for the same developer attention, yet they sit at very different points on the hardware ladder. Choosing among them is harder than the headlines suggest. Parameter counts run from small on-device variants to a model that Moonshot describes at the 3-trillion level, and “open” means something different in each license file. Readers who want the licensing side in isolation can start with our [open-weight license comparison](https://shattered.io/open-weight-models-license-comparison-6-families-16gb-2026/). The narrower question is which of these models should actually sit behind your editor, terminal agent or CI job. The short answer, with the evidence below. For a single developer with a 16 GB-class machine, gpt-oss-20b is the safest starting point because OpenAI ships it under Apache 2.0 and documents a small memory footprint. For a team with an 80 GB-class workstation, gpt-oss-120b is the next step up. Gemma 4 is the pick when you want the cleanest license and a size for every machine. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a server-class model, not a laptop model. DeepSeek, Qwen and Llama stay on the watch list because the evidence we could verify today does not support ranking them for local use. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The third reason got a live demonstration this week. On November 10, 2026, DigitalOcean published a release note that [pulled several open models from its serverless inference product](https://docs.digitalocean.com/notes/2026/inference-deprecate-oss-models-nov-2026/). A hosting decision simply removed a cheap endpoint, and every team that had wired a pipeline to it had to migrate. Weights on your own disk do not get deprecated that way. highlights.content: Alibaba opened Qwen4-Max-Preview to paying subscribers, the first model of its Qwen4 generation, at 9:00 p.m. ET on Nov. 10 (10:00 a.m. Nov. 11 in Beijing), and it will retire the model at 11:00 a.m. ET on Nov. 25, the day before Thanksgiving. Developers get two weeks to test a model with no published benchmarks or model card, and every prompt goes to a company subject to China's National Intelligence Law, whose Article 7 requires support. Scholars dispute how far that duty reaches data held overseas. Alibaba's documentation says the preview runs through 24:00 Beijing time on Nov. 25 and that "no changes will be made during this period." The model is then retired, and the Token Plan page names no replacement. Alibaba's previous flagship offers a precedent but not a promise: Qwen3.8-Max opened as a preview on July 19, reached general availability on Aug. 3 and received open weights on Aug. 12. Neurohive reports that Alibaba has given no date for a full Qwen4-Max release. The model accepts text, images and video, offers a 1-million-token context window and can generate up to 393,216 tokens per response, a ceiling that reasoning and the final answer share. It works through the OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages formats, so tools including Claude Code and Cursor can connect to it, along with Qwen Code, Qoder and OpenClaw. Alibaba's documentation lists text, image and video inputs and names no other output type, so "multimodal" here means multimodal input. Alibaba has published no benchmark table, model card, parameter count, license, weights or per-token price for the model, according to OrcaRouter's Qwen4 lineup page, which leaves every quality claim with Alibaba itself. The Qwen team says early access also runs in QwenWork, Qoder, the Qwen app and QwenStudio. ### Reasoning Tokens Now Count Against max\_tokens, So Ported Qwen Limits Can Truncate Answers In the OpenAI Chat Completions format, max\_tokens equals max\_completion\_tokens for this model and caps thinking and the visible answer together. Alibaba warns that a limit previously sized for the answer alone may truncate output. The mechanism comes from how reasoning models spend compute. They generate chains of intermediate steps before the final answer, and hosted services meter those hidden steps as metered reasoning tokens. Alibaba bills thinking content as output tokens and returns it in a separate reasoning\_content field. OpenAI documents the same accounting for its own models and warns that a response can hit its cap before any visible output appears. Alibaba's page warns of truncation and does not describe that empty-answer case. Default settings raise the odds of hitting the cap. Thinking is on by default, reasoning\_effort defaults to xhigh with low and medium available, and Alibaba says not to set reasoning\_effort and thinking\_budget together. The thinking\_budget parameter caps reasoning tokens, and once the cap is reached the model starts its answer. Chat Completions also turns on preserve\_thinking by default, which sends earlier reasoning back in each assistant message, and Alibaba's documentation says preserved reasoning counts toward input tokens and billing. In a long agent session, that adds earlier reasoning to the input of every later turn. More reasoning tends to improve accuracy on hard problems at the price of cost and latency, and one study on the AIME math benchmark found reasoning models 10 to 74 times more expensive than non-reasoning counterparts. A default of xhigh therefore favors quality and burns the shared budget fastest. For reference, OpenAI recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning and output when first working with its reasoning models; that figure describes OpenAI's models, not Qwen4-Max-Preview, and it shows how large the reasoning share can be. AI Agents.content: # Kazakhstan-linked hackers used AI agent to spy on Central Asian governments Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers used an artificial intelligence agent to help spy on Central Asian governments, steal sensitive documents and infiltrate critical infrastructure networks, according to new research. Singapore-based cybersecurity firm CloudSEK uncovered the operation after discovering an exposed server belonging to Silent Lynx, a hacking group previously linked to espionage campaigns targeting Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Armenia, Belarus and Russia. The server contained more than a dozen gigabytes of data, including stolen government documents, hacking tools and records showing how an attacker used an AI agent to automate parts of the operation. According to the report published Wednesday, the operator relied on Hermes, an open-source AI agent configured to act as an offensive cybersecurity expert. The system primarily used AI models developed by Chinese company DeepSeek. Unlike conventional chatbots, AI agents can execute commands, run software and carry out tasks on behalf of their users. The agent helped with reconnaissance, data collection and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems, researchers said. It was also configured to execute certain potentially destructive commands without requiring additional approval. The operator communicated with the agent in Russian and connected it to a Telegram bot, allowing the hacker to issue instructions remotely from a phone. ## Government networks compromised One of the group's most significant intrusions targeted Tajikistan, where the hackers maintained extensive access to the national railway network from at least mid-August through early October. After breaking into the network, the attackers gained access to several servers, extracted databases containing login credentials and stole internal documents and operational reports. The hackers also gained access to a much broader collection of government information. Using the credentials of a single railway employee, they logged into Tajikistan's national electronic document management platform, which government ministries and agencies use to exchange official correspondence. The group developed automated tools to download large quantities of files, including thousands of documents sent to or processed by Tajikistan's Defense Ministry in 2026. The stolen material also included correspondence associated with the National Guard, the State Committee for National Security and the State Investment Committee, as well as information about more than 100 government organizations and their employees. CloudSEK also found evidence the group had compromised a server supporting Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative, a government platform used to monitor and manage forest resources. Additionally, the exposed server contained malicious files disguised as official documents from Turkmenistan, including a railway ticket and a regional government report. The files were created and tested in October, suggesting the group was preparing another phishing campaign. Researchers did not establish whether the attacks against Turkmenistan had succeeded. CloudSEK assessed with medium confidence that Silent Lynx has ties to Kazakhstan, citing Russian-language communications and test connections originating from a residential internet provider in the country. Those findings support earlier assessments by cybersecurity researchers that the group is likely based in Kazakhstan, although they do not establish any connection to the Kazakh government. Also tracked as Cavalry Werewolf and YoroTrooper, Silent Lynx has been active since at least 2022 and has previously targeted government agencies, diplomatic organizations and other institutions across Central Asia, Russia and Europe. AI Agents.titleZh: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands | TechCrunch
AI Agents.content: Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results. Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research. Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically. Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult. Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords. Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular. Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets. “Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.” Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals. Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers. The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents. This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic. AI Agents.content: [![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Gaijin-small.jpg) ![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Gaijin-mid.jpg) ![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Gaijin-large.jpg)](https://bit.ly/4uQ9EHS) [![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Gaijin-small.jpg) ![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Gaijin-mid.jpg) ![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Gaijin-large.jpg)](https://bit.ly/4uQ9EHS) [AI](https://wccftech.com/topic/ai/) [Hardware](https://wccftech.com/topic/hardware/) [Launch](https://wccftech.com/topic/launch/) # ASUS Aims To Turn Desktops Into A Local AI “Agent Computer” With New Hardware And Software Ecosystem [Sarfraz Khan](https://wccftech.com/author/sarfraz/) • [Comments](#comments "View comments") [![](https://www.gstatic.com/images/branding/productlogos/googleg_gradient/v1/24px.svg) Add to Preferred Sources](javascript:void(0)) Vendors like ASUS are now expanding their Agent Computer initiative across DIY PCs, gaming systems, workstations, and creator machines. ## ASUS Expands its Agent Computer Ecosystem to Bring Local AI and AI Agents to DIY PCs, Gaming Systems, and Workstations Popular hardware maker ASUS is pushing its AI strategy beyond traditional AI PCs as it introduces the **Agent Computer** initiative designed to make local and agentic AI accessible to a variety of desktop hardware. The company says users will be able to choose between local, cloud, and hybrid AI depending on their performance, privacy, and cost requirements. [##### **Related Story** AMD Acknowledges Radeon Driver Bug Causing Constant SSD Writes, Fix In The Works](https://wccftech.com/amd-acknowledges-radeon-driver-bug-causing-constant-ssd-writes-fix-in-the-works/) The initiative covers everything from DIY PCs built using ASUS motherboards and the modern NVIDIA RTX or AMD Radeon AI GPUs to mini PCs, eGPU accelerators, and even enterprise-class systems. ASUS says its PRIME, TUF Gaming, ROG, and ProArt motherboard families can become the foundation for these systems, and ExpertCenter Pro workstations such as the ET900A X9 will target more demanding workloads. The company also launched "Find Your ASUS Agent Computer" on the official website, which allows users to choose between "Local and Hybrid" and "Cloud" and suggests a computer or components based on individual needs. ASUS's new approach is particularly interesting since it has been developing hardware specifically designed around local AI. Devices such as the [ProArt GR1X mini PC use NVIDIA's RTX Spark platform](https://wccftech.com/asus-proart-gr1x-rtx-spark-mini-pc-1440p-100fps-140w/), which runs on a 6,144-core Blackwell GPU, a 20-core Grace CPU, and up to 128 GB of unified memory. The mini PC can run large AI models and agentic workflows locally, including models with up to 120 billion parameters. [ASUS has also recently launched its XG Core external GPU](https://wccftech.com/asus-launches-xg-core-radeon-rx-9060-xt-lp-external-graphics-card/), powered by a low-profile Radeon RX 9060 XT with 16 GB of VRAM, which can provide local AI acceleration for laptops, in addition to offering a high-performance gaming experience for mobile devices. ![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-mobile.png) ![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-desktop.png) ASUS is also developing software such as **Zenni Claw**, which brings agentic AI capabilities to consumer devices, and **Multi-LM Tuner,** which helps users deploy optimized large language models across ASUS platforms. Moreover, the company is also deploying **DisplayWidget Center** as a bridge between ASUS displays and emerging AI workflows. LLMs.titleZh: Best Local LLM for Coding: $0 Weights vs $2 API [2026]
LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Best Local LLM for Coding: $0 Weights vs $2 API [2026] ![Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/tvance.webp) [Tom Vance](https://shattered.io/author/tvance/) Updated Nov 12, 2026 · 26 min read The best local LLM for coding in mid-November 2026 depends less on a leaderboard score than on three constraints: how much memory your machine has, what license the weights carry, and whether you can verify the files you download. Google’s [Gemma 4 family, released under Apache 2.0 with commercial use allowed](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemma-4/), OpenAI’s gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b, and Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro all compete for the same developer attention, yet they sit at very different points on the hardware ladder. Choosing among them is harder than the headlines suggest. Parameter counts run from small on-device variants to a model that Moonshot describes at the 3-trillion level, and “open” means something different in each license file. Readers who want the licensing side in isolation can start with our [open-weight license comparison](https://shattered.io/open-weight-models-license-comparison-6-families-16gb-2026/). The narrower question is which of these models should actually sit behind your editor, terminal agent or CI job. The short answer, with the evidence below. For a single developer with a 16 GB-class machine, gpt-oss-20b is the safest starting point because OpenAI ships it under Apache 2.0 and documents a small memory footprint. For a team with an 80 GB-class workstation, gpt-oss-120b is the next step up. Gemma 4 is the pick when you want the cleanest license and a size for every machine. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a server-class model, not a laptop model. DeepSeek, Qwen and Llama stay on the watch list because the evidence we could verify today does not support ranking them for local use. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Why Run a Coding Model on Your Own Hardware in November 2026 Three reasons keep pulling developers toward local inference: code privacy, cost predictability and independence from someone else’s deprecation calendar. The third reason got a live demonstration this week. On November 10, 2026, DigitalOcean published a release note that [pulled several open models from its serverless inference product](https://docs.digitalocean.com/notes/2026/inference-deprecate-oss-models-nov-2026/). The notice names Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct, and a research summary of the same notice reports that Gemma 4, Qwen 3.5 397B A17B and DeepSeek V4 Flash left serverless inference too, with DigitalOcean pointing users toward DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Gemma 4 stayed available on dedicated inference. Nothing was discontinued by its maker. A hosting decision simply removed a cheap endpoint, and every team that had wired a pipeline to it had to migrate. Weights on your own disk do not get deprecated that way. If you pin a model file and a runtime version, the behavior of your coding assistant stays the same next month, which matters when your test suite or your review bot depends on consistent output. That stability is the strongest practical argument for local, stronger than raw price. ### What the industry data says about open models Adoption data points the same direction, though unevenly. LLMs.title: Alibaba Qwen4-Max-Preview Retires November 25 With No Benchmarks, Model Card or Price
LLMs.titleZh: Alibaba Qwen4-Max-Preview Retires November 25 With No Benchmarks, Model Card or Price
LLMs.content: Alibaba opened Qwen4-Max-Preview to paying subscribers, the first model of its Qwen4 generation, at 9:00 p.m. ET on Nov. 10 (10:00 a.m. Nov. 11 in Beijing), and it will retire the model at 11:00 a.m. ET on Nov. 25, the day before Thanksgiving. Developers get two weeks to test a model with no published benchmarks or model card, and every prompt goes to a company subject to China's National Intelligence Law, whose Article 7 requires support. Scholars dispute how far that duty reaches data held overseas. Alibaba's documentation says the preview runs through 24:00 Beijing time on Nov. 25 and that "no changes will be made during this period." The model is then retired, and the Token Plan page names no replacement. Alibaba's previous flagship offers a precedent but not a promise: Qwen3.8-Max opened as a preview on July 19, reached general availability on Aug. 3 and received open weights on Aug. 12. Neurohive reports that Alibaba has given no date for a full Qwen4-Max release. The model accepts text, images and video, offers a 1-million-token context window and can generate up to 393,216 tokens per response, a ceiling that reasoning and the final answer share. It works through the OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages formats, so tools including Claude Code and Cursor can connect to it, along with Qwen Code, Qoder and OpenClaw. Alibaba's documentation lists text, image and video inputs and names no other output type, so "multimodal" here means multimodal input. Alibaba has published no benchmark table, model card, parameter count, license, weights or per-token price for the model, according to OrcaRouter's Qwen4 lineup page, which leaves every quality claim with Alibaba itself. The Qwen team says early access also runs in QwenWork, Qoder, the Qwen app and QwenStudio. ### Reasoning Tokens Now Count Against max\_tokens, So Ported Qwen Limits Can Truncate Answers In the OpenAI Chat Completions format, max\_tokens equals max\_completion\_tokens for this model and caps thinking and the visible answer together. Alibaba warns that a limit previously sized for the answer alone may truncate output. The mechanism comes from how reasoning models spend compute. They generate chains of intermediate steps before the final answer, and hosted services meter those hidden steps as metered reasoning tokens. Alibaba bills thinking content as output tokens and returns it in a separate reasoning\_content field. OpenAI documents the same accounting for its own models and warns that a response can hit its cap before any visible output appears. Alibaba's page warns of truncation and does not describe that empty-answer case. Default settings raise the odds of hitting the cap. Thinking is on by default, reasoning\_effort defaults to xhigh with low and medium available, and Alibaba says not to set reasoning\_effort and thinking\_budget together. The thinking\_budget parameter caps reasoning tokens, and once the cap is reached the model starts its answer. Chat Completions also turns on preserve\_thinking by default, which sends earlier reasoning back in each assistant message, and Alibaba's documentation says preserved reasoning counts toward input tokens and billing. In a long agent session, that adds earlier reasoning to the input of every later turn. More reasoning tends to improve accuracy on hard problems at the price of cost and latency, and one study on the AIME math benchmark found reasoning models 10 to 74 times more expensive than non-reasoning counterparts. A default of xhigh therefore favors quality and burns the shared budget fastest. For reference, OpenAI recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning and output when first working with its reasoning models; that figure describes OpenAI's models, not Qwen4-Max-Preview, and it shows how large the reasoning share can be. Testing at low and medium effort shows how many tokens reasoning consumes on your own tasks. Alibaba has not described Qwen4-Max-Preview's archit...

AI News # Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Who Gets It, What It Costs, and How It Compares By [Lenka Vojtechova](/author/lenka-vojtechova/)  ·  Updated November 12, 2026  ·  13 min read [Gemini](/tag/gemini/)[Google](/tag/google/)[DeepMind](/tag/deepmind/)[AI Model Review](/tag/ai-model-review/)[AI Pricing](/tag/ai-pricing/)[LLM](/tag/llm/) ![Glowing Gemini sparkle app icon on a blue and purple background next to the text Gemini 4 Hydrogen: who gets it free?](/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/gemini-4-hydrogen-hero.webp) Google released **Gemini 4 Hydrogen** on **November 12, 2026**, and it is the first Gemini 4 model that does not cost anything to try. Hydrogen scores **51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index**, one point above Gemini 4 Argon, at **$1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens**. Google built it as the fast, everyday model of the Gemini 4 family, and it replaces Gemini 3.8 Flash as the model Google tells developers to move to. Google's headline promises Gemini 4 for everyone, but who actually gets Hydrogen depends on where you look. Developers get a real free tier. Free Gemini app users only get Hydrogen when Google's Auto mode decides a prompt needs it. This guide covers what Hydrogen is, who gets it on each plan and what it costs against 3.8 Flash, Argon and Carbon. It also shows where its benchmarks hold up, and where Claude Sonnet 5.5 still wins. ## The Key Takeaways > * **Released November 12, 2026:** Gemini 4 Hydrogen is Google's fast Gemini 4 model, **adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon**, and the recommended upgrade from Gemini 3.8 Flash. > * **Free, with a catch:** the Gemini API and Google AI Studio have a **free tier for Hydrogen**, a first for Gemini 4. In the Gemini app, free users get it only through Auto. Picking it yourself starts with **Google AI Plus at $4.99 a month**. > * **Price:** **$1.50 / $7.50** per million tokens. That is double 3.8 Flash today, but 3.8 Flash rises to the same rate on **January 1, 2027**. > * **Benchmarks:** **51** on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at default settings and **54** at xhigh, against 31 for 3.8 Flash. Artificial Analysis spent **$1.87 per index task against $7.77** for 3.8 Flash. > * **Where it loses:** Claude Sonnet 5.5 beats it on **Terminal-Bench 4.1 (63.9% vs 57.0%)**, OSWorld-2.1 and Terminal-Bench-Science in Google's own table. ## What Is Gemini 4 Hydrogen? It appears to be the counterpart to the earlier Flash series. That comparison may sell it short, though. The software is intended to act as a single layer for managing AI activity, costs, identity and oversight across different models, tools and teams. It forms part of Globant's broader AI services approach, which combines software with human-supervised delivery teams known as AI Pods. Glob.AI OS connects to more than 320 open and closed AI models from more than 25 providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The system can direct tasks to different models while giving companies visibility into spending, usage and policy controls. The product is built around four parts: an Intelligence Hub for model access and routing, a Corporate Hub for linking company data and systems, an Agentic Hub for testing and running AI agents, and a Token Vault for budgets, permissions and audit records. It can be deployed as software as a service or within a client's own cloud environment. Access is available through chat, web, desktop and command-line interfaces, as well as through headless deployment using MCP. AI Product.content: IT Brief New Zealand - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief New Zealand logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg) New Zealand](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.nz) ![Nol8 launches AI data plane for enterprise controls](https://itbrief.co.nz/uploads/story/2026/11/12/sanjeev-mohan-story-324319.webp) [Data governance](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/data-governance) [Risk & Compliance](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/risk-compliance) [ERP](https://itbrief.co.nz/tag/enterprise-resource-planning) # Nol8 launches AI data plane for enterprise controls Fri, 13th Nov 2026 (Today) [![Sean Mitchell](https://itbrief.co.nz/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](/author/sean-mitchell) Nol8 has launched its AI Data Plane for commercial use, aimed at companies seeking tighter control over what data reaches artificial intelligence systems. The platform sits between enterprise data and AI workloads, inspecting data moving into and out of models, agents and tools. It reviews prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls, agent-to-agent exchanges and model outputs, then applies company-defined rules to decide what can pass through. The launch comes as businesses shift from testing AI tools to deploying larger numbers of autonomous agents across their operations. That shift is prompting closer scrutiny of how companies govern sensitive information exposed to models during routine tasks. Nol8 says its approach relies on deterministic pattern matching rather than probabilistic controls. That means the same rule should produce the same result on every request, with requests blocked if the platform is unreachable rather than allowed through. Benchmark results released alongside the launch compared the product with a CPU-based baseline built on Google RE2, a pattern-matching engine. Nol8 says the testing was independently validated and found that its system processed more than 100 times more data per dollar at the top end of the policy range examined. In the tests, policy size increased from 128 rules to 5,000 rules. Across that range, Nol8 says its platform sustained throughput of 1 GB/s, while the RE2 baseline slowed by 30 times as rule volumes increased. The company argues this matters because the cost of inspecting AI traffic can rise sharply as organisations add more policies. For businesses trying to govern growing volumes of AI interactions, the economics of inspection infrastructure are becoming part of the adoption debate. Industry forecasts cited by Nol8 point to sharp growth in agent use. Gartner has forecast that by 2028 the average global Fortune 500 company will have more than 150,000 AI agents in use, up from fewer than 15 in 2025, while IDC has projected a tenfold increase in agent use across the Global 2000 by 2027. **Security focus** Unlike traditional data governance systems centred on stored information, Nol8 is targeting what it describes as data in motion. That includes the live flow of information through prompts, context retrieval, software tool calls and exchanges between agents. Kelly Herrell, Chief Executive Officer of Nol8, said the issue starts with data access rather than model behaviour. "Most of the conversation about enterprise AI has focused on whether it behaves correctly. Before behavior comes a more basic question: what data does AI actually access? AI needs broad access to be useful, and that access expands every day as AI pushes deeper into the business," Herrell said. Open Source AI.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Edge0 releases open-source 145-billion-parameter model for local inference on laptops](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fedge0-releases-open-source-145-billion-parameter-model-for-local-inference-on-laptops_gen_1794530938866-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # Edge0 releases open-source 145-billion-parameter model for local inference on laptops • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article Advertisement [Advertise on LavX NewsSee options](/advertise) Edge0 published weights for Edge0-145B and Edge0-120B, an inference framework, and deployment tools, claiming laptop-scale local performance on coding and agent tasks. The reported gains depend on internal evaluations and hardware-specific measurements that outside testers still need to reproduce. Edge0 released [Edge0-145B](https://edge0.ai/blog/introducing-edge0-145b-frontier-ai-capabilities-on-your-own-computer), a 145-billion-parameter language model the company says runs on a personal computer. The release includes Edge0-120B, an inference framework, deployment tools, and model weights on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co), with code and guides on [GitHub](https://github.com). Edge0 positions the models for coding, reasoning, and agent workflows without sending prompts to a cloud model. ## What's claimed Edge0 describes Edge0-145B as an open-source on-device model with 145 billion parameters and performance near specific frontier cloud models. In the company's laptop tests, the model reached peak memory of 29 gigabytes, prompt processing above 1,100 tokens per second, generation above 80 tokens per second, and power draw near 120 watts. Edge0 reports support for 128,000 to 256,000 tokens of context on long inputs. Edge0 also claims the model can complete multi-step work on a local machine. The company points to demonstrations in which Edge0-145B planned tasks, wrote and ran code, debugged failures, and inspected results. Examples include 3D scenes in Blender, game assets, drone control code, and a printed circuit board workflow in KiCad and Unreal Engine 5. ## What's new The release combines model architecture and inference engineering aimed at the limits of laptop memory and bandwidth. Edge0 says it shares large matrices across groups of sparse experts, trains the model in its on-device form from the start, pipelines data across GPU memory, system memory, and SSD storage, and splits work between the CPU and GPU with speculative decoding. Of the 145 billion parameters, Edge0 reports that about 10 billion participate in each inference step. Edge0 presents benchmark results from its internal evaluations. In the company's table, Edge0-145B scores 64.6 on DeepSWE 1.1, 86.52 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 35.4 on HLE, 90.4 on GPQA-Diamond, 80.6 on IFBench, and 79.3 on AA-LCR. Edge0 compares those scores with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, and Claude-Opus-4.6 (Max), with gaps in published results marked by dashes. The memory comparison stands out. Edge0 says this makes the model usable on a 48-gigabyte laptop. The company states that it will release the evaluation setup, hardware environment, and reproduction instructions with a technical report. Edge0 frames local inference as a way to avoid cloud-model token or API fees, keep code and documents on the user's hardware, and continue core tasks offline. Open Source AI.content: [Home](/en) Article # 4K Image Generation in 10 Seconds: MiniMax Unveils New Open-Source SOTA Again 机器之心2026-11-13 07:54 GPT is cooked. "GPT is cooked." Over the past two days, this line has been repeatedly circulating across the AI community. What has everyone restless with excitement is the newly released image model from MiniMax, **MiniMax H3 Image**. This is a model that outputs native 4K images directly, completes generation in 10 seconds, and supports 16 reference images. It was just open-sourced this Tuesday, **setting a new SOTA for open-source image models**. Judging from the first wave of reactions from the community, this claim hardly sounds exaggerated at all. Developers who got early access to the internal beta have run a large number of tests. In the outputs of the new model, the "plastic-like artificial texture" that used to haunt AI-generated portraits is gone, with pores, freckles, and fine hairs all clearly visible. People are full of praise for its capabilities in game design, character setting, and 3D scene creation. On the Artificial Analysis ranking updated today, **MiniMax H3-Image ranks first among all open-weight models in both text-to-image and image editing categories**. MiniMax H3 Image supports direct use on the web, and can also be used via API in MiniMax Code or other harnesses to complete complex tasks. And since it is open-source, **some users have already started working on local deployment**. GitHub: https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-H3-Image HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image We got access to the new model as soon as possible, and tested it to show you its actual performance level. ## **Redefining Visual Aesthetics and "Sense of Realism"** This new model is already launched in MiniMax Code. When you open it, you will find it supports up to 16 reference images, and the generated images can reach a maximum resolution of 4K. From the perspective of an ordinary user, we tested the scenarios that people use in daily life across four capability dimensions: we first checked its realism performance, then tackled the two classic pain points of text rendering and human face generation, and finally tried secondary creation with image-to-image generation. **Realistic output is the first checkpoint**. The things that most easily expose AI traces are often the objects we look at every day, such as the WeChat chat interface. Prompt: Generate a realistic WeChat chat screenshot: I first send the other party a very realistic photo of a Coca-Cola, and say "This is generated by MiniMax H3 Image", the other party replies "Oh my god", then I say "Just kidding, I took this photo myself". Make sure the screenshot includes highly realistic details of the iPhone status bar, including time, battery level and signal strength. We only input this single prompt, and MiniMax H3 Image generates a complete WeChat chat screenshot right away. The reason why this kind of daily interface is hard to generate is that the human eye has an extremely low fault tolerance rate for familiar scenes. The WeChat interface has relatively fixed visual specifications: if the font is slightly thicker, the spacing of chat bubbles is off, or the proportion of status bar icons is incorrect, the flaw will be spotted immediately. When many models generate similar chat screenshots, either the interface elements are misplaced and deformed, or the product photos have unnatural highlights, which greatly reduces the sense of realism. In the images generated by MiniMax H3 Image, details including the iPhone status bar, WeChat UI layout, chat bubbles, and avatars are all quite in place. The Coca-Cola photo is also realistic enough, with natural condensation on the bottle body, light and shadow reflection, and desktop texture, leaving almost no trace of AI generation. Open Source AI.titleZh: AWS Open-Sources AI Agent Evaluation Framework That Hardens Its AI Grader Against Prompt Injection
Open Source AI.content: Amazon Web Services has open-sourced the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF), an evaluation system that scores AI agents the same way regardless of which framework built them. The code is released under Apache 2.0 on GitHub, and AWS announced it on November 11. It targets a persistent problem in production agent development: evaluation tooling is split by framework, so teams struggle to apply the same metrics across stacks or to tell whether a new release is better or worse than the last. UAEF also takes an unusual approach to the AI model that grades agents. AWS says the grader is built to treat everything an agent produces as untrusted input, so an agent cannot talk its way into a higher score. ### Why Agent Evaluation Has Been So Fragmented Teams building AI agents face a measurement problem that traditional software does not. When code ships, a regression suite either passes or fails. When an agent ships, the question is whether it reasoned, called tools and responded well across many quality dimensions, against a threshold that is never perfectly defined. That gets harder when a team runs agents on several frameworks, because each one records execution traces in a different format. LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Langfuse each name and structure trace fields differently. Without a normalization layer, applying one metric to traces from two frameworks needs custom glue code for every pair, a cost many teams avoid by never comparing across frameworks at all. UAEF defines one internal format, called ``` AgentTrace ``` , and writes an adapter for each framework that converts its native traces into that format. The evaluation engine then works only on ``` AgentTrace ``` objects. AWS's announcement names five framework adapters, and the adapters listed in its README also include Amazon Bedrock Agents and a generic JSON adapter for custom or homegrown frameworks. Read more: AI Agent Security Hits Its Reckoning: Prompt Injection May Be a Permanent Flaw, Not a Patchable Bug ### 36 Metrics in Two Scoring Modes UAEF ships 36 built-in metrics organized into seven dimensions: Response Quality, Tool Calling, Multi-Turn, Reasoning, Responsible AI, Multi-Agent and Performance. Each metric returns a score from 0 to 1. The metrics split into two scoring modes. Deterministic metrics compute scores from the trace and ground truth using code, so they reproduce identically on every run and need no model calls. Judge metrics prompt a model on Amazon Bedrock to score subjective qualities such as relevance, safety and faithfulness. Judge scores can vary slightly between runs of the same trace. Research shows why that matters. A June 2026 study by Norman, Rivera and Hughes found two production-deployed judges with test-retest reliability above 0.95 and position bias above 0.10, which the authors call a consistency-bias paradox: a judge can be consistent and still systematically skewed. A separate April 2026 paper found style bias dominant among the bias types it tested, far exceeding position bias, with judges favoring markdown formatting over plain prose. The UAEF documentation describes judge scores as evaluation signal rather than a safety decision, and recommends Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for runtime enforcement. Teams should read absolute judge values with that in mind and avoid using them as the sole gate on a release. Reference-based metrics are skipped automatically when no ground truth is supplied, which lowers the bar for evaluating live or synthetic traffic. ### How the Judge Is Hardened Against Prompt Injection The most distinctive part of UAEF is its judge design. An agent that reads a web page, document or tool response can pick up adversarial instructions and carry them into its output. If a judge receives that output pasted into one scoring prompt, it may follow the injected instructions instead of scoring the work. Open Source AI.title: MiniMax Releases Open-Weight Image Model H3-Image: Only Pricier Highspeed Tier Nears 10-Second 4K
Open Source AI.titleZh: MiniMax Releases Open-Weight Image Model H3-Image: Only Pricier Highspeed Tier Nears 10-Second 4K
Open Source AI.content: MiniMax's H3-Image, an open-weight image model whose weights reached Hugging Face on November 10, renders 4,096-by-4,096-pixel images in six sampling steps with no guidance pass, but the only median timings published so far put its fastest 4K tier at 10.3 seconds, not the under-10 seconds the company advertises. Developers weighing the model need to know which tier produces that number, what the six-step design removes, and that its license excludes four territories: the US, EU, UK and South Korea. The weights are on Hugging Face as ``` MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3-Image ``` and the code is on GitHub. Neither MiniMax's launch post nor the repository README publishes a technical report or benchmark scores. ### Reported Medians: 10.3 Seconds at Highspeed, 16.0 Seconds at Standard for 4K MiniMax's launch post says a 4K image arrives in under 10 seconds, at up to five times the speed of "mainstream alternatives" it does not name, with Standard mode 1.5 to 2 times as fast and Highspeed mode 3 to 4 times as fast. The post does not name the hardware behind the measurement, and its latency chart values do not appear in the text. The median API latencies reported by Neurohive are less dramatic: 4K task Standard Highspeed Text-to-image 16.0 s 10.3 s 1 reference 18.2 s 12.5 s 3 references 21.4 s 14.4 s On those figures, even Highspeed text-to-image sits 0.3 seconds above the claim. At 1K resolution, Standard mode (10.6 seconds) is slower than GPT-image 2.6 medium (9.0 seconds), and Neurohive notes that the competitor numbers come from MiniMax's original comparison while H3-Image was re-measured. OrcaRouter, an API-routing service, said on November 11 that no third-party timing had been published. The faster tier costs more. OrcaRouter lists 4K list prices of $0.06879 per image at Standard and $0.13001 at Highspeed, a ratio of about 1.9 to 1. A 50% discount on 4K output runs through November 17 at 16:00 UTC (11 a.m. ET) and applies only to images at 16.6 million pixels or larger. ### Six Steps, No Guidance Pass: Speed Locks In One Operating Point H3-Image is a 33.1-billion-parameter, dense, single-stream diffusion transformer with 50 layers, a hidden size of 5,376, 56 attention heads and 3D multimodal rotary position encoding. It descends from H3, the omni-modal video model MiniMax launched on July 31, with the audio layers removed. The repository says the checkpoint is distilled to six function evaluations and uses no classifier-free guidance. In a conventional guided diffusion model, each sampling step evaluates two networks, one conditioned on the prompt and one unconditioned, and a sampler repeats that pair tens to hundreds of times. Published research on distilling guided models has produced images in 1 to 4 steps for latent-space models such as Stable Diffusion. MiniMax has not said which distillation method it used, and its launch post describes post-training broadly. With guidance built into the weights, each step needs one network evaluation rather than two. That design fixes the operating point. The repository accepts only six steps and a guidance scale of 1, and other values return HTTP 400; the hosted API fixes the same settings. Negative prompts are not supported. A user who finds a weak result cannot raise the step count or the guidance scale to chase more fidelity, so the quoted speed and the quality ceiling are one setting, not two. The upside is that fixed settings should make outputs reproducible, though that is an untested expectation. Text conditioning reuses the full Qwen3-VL encoder from H3 unchanged, and the diffusion transformer reads hidden states from its layer 50. Text and reference-image tokens share one sequence, so a single checkpoint handles text-to-image and multi-image editing with up to 16 references, and prompts are truncated at 4,096 tokens. One caveat: one serving recipe documents nine images per request, so the full 16 may not be available on every runtime. ### Sixteen-Times VAE Compression Turns 4K Image Int...

Open Source AI.titleZh: Open-Source AI Coding Assistant Audit: 12 Steps [2026]
Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) # Open-Source AI Coding Audit: 12 Steps, 80 Min [2026] ![Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/lbennett.webp) [Laura Bennett](https://shattered.io/author/lbennett/) Updated Nov 12, 2026 · 38 min read Developers now hand their repositories to AI assistants by default. The [Stack Overflow 2025 Developer Survey](https://stackoverflow.co/company/press/archive/stack-overflow-2025-developer-survey) found that 84% of respondents use or plan to use AI tools in their development process, and 51% of professional developers use them daily. An open-source AI coding assistant sounds like the safe pick in that world, because you can read the source. Reading the source and knowing what the installed build does on your machine are two different things. A repeatable audit takes about 80 minutes to run against any open-source coding assistant: license and maintenance checks, telemetry inventory, a logging proxy, canary secrets, an approval-prompt test, a prompt-injection probe and a locked-down container. If you already followed an [Aider local setup with Ollama and Git](https://shattered.io/aider-local-ai-coding-assistant-ollama-git-2026/), you have a working assistant. Now you will find out what it sends, where it sends it and what it is allowed to touch. The examples use Cline (editor extension and CLI) and Aider, because both are active open-source projects that accept your own model or API key. Every step works for other tools too. A [Cline setup walkthrough](https://shattered.io/cline-ai-setup-vscode-cli-12-steps-2026/) covers installation. Here the goal is evidence: numbers and logs you can show a security reviewer or a teammate before the tool goes near a production repo. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## What an Open-Source AI Coding Assistant Audit Checks, and What You Need First An open-source license tells you the code is inspectable. It does not tell you how often the maintainers ship, whether the project still has maintainers, which hosts the binary calls, whether it phones home when you turn telemetry off, or what it does when a README tells it to run a shell command. The audit answers six questions, and each one maps to a step later in the tutorial. First, is the project alive and under a license you can live with? Second, what telemetry and update checks ship by default? Third, which network destinations does the assistant contact during a task, and how many bytes does it send to each? Fourth, do your secrets leave the machine when the assistant reads the working tree? Fifth, which actions run without a prompt? Sixth, does the assistant resist instructions planted inside the files it reads? Maintenance deserves the first slot because it changes fast. Continue, a popular VS Code assistant, is a recent example. Secondary sources report that Cursor acquired it in June 2026, that the hosted service shut down and that the repository went read-only, so treat it as unmaintained code you could fork rather than a living product. That reading comes from a [third-party profile](https://tomrochette.com/agents/surfaces/continue/) and I could not confirm it on an official page, which is exactly why the audit asks you to check the repository yourself. The announcement positions the company as a serious alternative to Nvidia in the red-hot AI infrastructure market, where demand for specialized chips continues to outpace supply. [Cerebras Systems](https://cerebras.net) just proved the AI chip market has room for more than one winner. The Sunnyvale-based company sent its stock soaring 18% in extended trading after reporting third-quarter revenue that beat Wall Street expectations and dropping news of a partnership with [Microsoft](https://microsoft.com) that puts its wafer-scale chips into Azure data centers. The Microsoft deal marks a turning point for Cerebras, which now counts all three hyperscale cloud giants as customers.
